title: Observability & logging
summary: Make your app explain itself in production using structured logs, request IDs, metrics, and traces so you can find problems fast.
objectives: Understand the three pillars of observability: logs, metrics, and traces
Use Python's logging module with levels instead of print statements
Write structured (JSON) logs so machines can search and filter them
Attach request IDs and context to follow one request across your code
Track latency, token usage, and errors for LLM API calls
Avoid logging secrets and other sensitive data
Know when to reach for a tool like Sentry or a metrics dashboard

quiz.q: Which Python module is the standard, built-in way to record what your program is doing?
quiz.why: The logging module ships with Python and gives you levels, formatting, and configurable destinations that print cannot.

quiz.q: Put these log levels in order from least to most severe: ERROR, DEBUG, INFO, WARNING.
quiz.why: DEBUG is the most detailed and least severe; ERROR signals something genuinely went wrong. CRITICAL sits above ERROR.

quiz.q: Why are structured (JSON) logs better than plain text logs for a deployed app?
options: Machines can search, filter, and aggregate the fields
quiz.why: Each log becomes key-value data, so tools can query by request_id, level, or latency instead of grepping raw strings.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of attaching a request ID to every log line for a single request?
quiz.answer: It lets you trace one request's whole journey through your code, even when many requests run at once.
quiz.why: A shared correlation ID ties scattered log lines together so you can follow exactly what happened for one user's call.

quiz.q: Which of these should you NEVER write into a log?
options: A user's API key or password
quiz.why: Logs are often stored and shared widely; secrets and credentials must never be written to them.

quiz.q: For an LLM-powered endpoint, name two numbers worth logging on every call.
quiz.answer: Latency and token usage (input and output tokens); error rate is also valuable.
quiz.why: Latency and tokens drive your cost and user experience, so tracking them per call lets you spot slow or expensive requests.

body_markdown:
## Why observability?

On your laptop you can watch your program run. In production you cannot — it runs on a server somewhere, serving real users, and the first sign of trouble is often an angry message. **Observability** is the practice of making your app explain itself: emitting enough signal that you can answer *what happened?* and *why?* without redeploying.

It rests on three pillars: **logs** (a timestamped record of events), **metrics** (numbers over time, like requests per minute), and **traces** (the path of one request through your system).

## Logging properly: stop using print

`print()` is fine while you write code, but it has no levels, no timestamps, and no easy way to switch off. Python's built-in `logging` module fixes all of that.

```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

log.info("Server started")
log.warning("Cache miss for user %s", user_id)
log.error("Payment failed", exc_info=True)
```

**Levels** let you control noise: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. In production you might show INFO and above; while debugging you drop to DEBUG.

## Structured logs

Plain-text logs are readable by humans but painful for machines. **Structured logging** emits each line as JSON, so a log platform can filter by any field.

```python
import json, logging, time

def log_event(**fields):
    fields["ts"] = time.time()
    print(json.dumps(fields))

log_event(level="INFO", event="llm_call", model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
          latency_ms=842, input_tokens=120, output_tokens=210)
```

Now you can ask your tooling "show me every `llm_call` slower than 2000ms" instead of grepping raw text.

## Request IDs: following one request

When many requests run at once, their log lines interleave. Attach a **request ID** (a correlation ID) to every line for a request, and you can follow that one request end to end.

```python
import uuid, logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def handle(request):
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    log.info("received", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    # ... do work, passing request_id everywhere ...
    log.info("completed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
```

## Observability for LLM calls

LLM endpoints have their own signals worth tracking: **latency**, **token usage** (which drives cost), and **errors**. Wrap each Claude call and log the outcome.

```python
import time, logging
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

start = time.perf_counter()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this ticket."}],
)
latency_ms = round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
log.info("llm_call ok latency_ms=%s in=%s out=%s",
         latency_ms, msg.usage.input_tokens, msg.usage.output_tokens)
```

## Don't log secrets, and reach for tools

Logs get stored, copied, and shared — so **never** write API keys, passwords, tokens, or full user data into them. Redact or omit them.

Once your logs are structured, dedicated tools earn their keep: **Sentry** captures and groups exceptions with full stack traces; a metrics dashboard charts latency and error rates over time. Start with good logs, then layer tools on top.

## Your task

Take one endpoint from your project and add structured logging with a request ID, plus latency and token logging on any LLM call.

slides.narration: Welcome to Month Five, where we polish, deploy, and go public. In this lesson we tackle observability and logging. Once your app runs on a server instead of your laptop, you can't just watch it work. So we'll make the app explain itself, so that when something breaks at two in the morning, you can find out exactly what happened, fast.

slides.title: Why observability?
bullets: On a server you can't watch your code run.
Observability makes the app explain itself.
Answer: what happened, and why?
Find problems without redeploying.
slides.narration: Here's the core problem. On your laptop, you can see your program run and print things out. In production it runs somewhere you can't see, serving real users. Observability is the practice of making your app emit enough signal that you can answer what happened and why, after the fact, without having to redeploy and reproduce the bug yourself.

slides.title: The three pillars
bullets: Logs: timestamped record of events.
Metrics: numbers over time, like requests per minute.
Traces: the path of one request through the system.
Most apps start with logs.
slides.narration: Observability rests on three pillars. Logs are a timestamped record of events: this happened, then that happened. Metrics are numbers measured over time, like requests per minute or error rate. Traces follow a single request as it moves through your system. Most apps begin with solid logs, then add metrics and traces as they grow.

slides.title: Stop using print
bullets: print has no levels, no timestamps, no off switch.
Python's logging module fixes all of that.
Levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL.
Show the noise you want, hide the rest.
slides.code:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("Server started")
log.error("Payment failed", exc_info=True)
slides.narration: Print is fine while you write code, but it has no levels, no timestamps, and no easy way to switch off. Python's built-in logging module fixes all of that. You get five levels, from DEBUG, the most detailed, up to CRITICAL, the most severe. In production you might show INFO and above; while debugging you drop down to DEBUG to see everything.

slides.title: Log levels in order
bullets: DEBUG: fine detail for diagnosing.
INFO: normal events worth noting.
WARNING: something odd but recoverable.
ERROR and CRITICAL: something broke.
slides.narration: Let's pin down the levels, because the quiz will ask. From least to most severe: DEBUG is the fine-grained detail you use while diagnosing. INFO is normal, healthy events. WARNING means something looked odd but the app carried on. ERROR means an operation genuinely failed, and CRITICAL sits above that for the worst cases. Choosing the right level is what keeps your logs useful instead of noisy.

slides.title: Structured logs
bullets: Plain text is readable, but hard to query.
Emit each log line as JSON instead.
Then filter by any field: level, latency, model.
Machines can search and aggregate them.
slides.code:
import json, time
def log_event(**fields):
    fields["ts"] = time.time()
    print(json.dumps(fields))

log_event(level="INFO", event="llm_call", latency_ms=842)
slides.narration: Plain text logs read nicely for a human but are painful for a machine. Structured logging emits each line as Jason, so every value becomes a searchable field. Now you can ask your tooling, show me every L L M call slower than two thousand milliseconds, instead of grepping through raw strings. This is the single biggest upgrade you can make to your logging.

slides.title: Request IDs
bullets: Many requests run at once; their logs interleave.
Attach one request ID to every line of a request.
Now you can follow that request end to end.
Also called a correlation ID.
slides.code:
import uuid
request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
log.info("received", extra={"request_id": request_id})
# ... pass request_id through your code ...
log.info("completed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
slides.narration: When many requests run at the same time, their log lines get tangled together. The fix is a request I D, sometimes called a correlation I D: generate a unique I D at the start of each request and attach it to every log line for that request. Then, even in a busy system, you can filter by that one I D and watch a single request's whole journey through your code.

slides.title: Observe your LLM calls
bullets: Track latency: how long the call took.
Track token usage: it drives your cost.
Track errors: did the call fail?
Wrap each call and log the outcome.
slides.code:
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
msg = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024, messages=msgs)
ms = round((time.perf_counter()-start)*1000)
log.info("llm_call ok ms=%s out=%s", ms, msg.usage.output_tokens)
slides.narration: Your A I endpoints have their own signals worth watching. Latency tells you how long the call took, which shapes the user experience. Token usage drives your cost, so log the input and output tokens from the usage object. And track errors, so you know when a call fails. Wrap each Claude call, time it, and log the outcome. Notice we read tokens straight off the message's usage field.

slides.title: Never log secrets
bullets: Logs get stored, copied, and shared widely.
Never write API keys, passwords, or tokens.
Redact or omit sensitive user data.
Keep keys in environment variables, not logs.
slides.narration: One rule you must not break: never log secrets. Logs get stored, copied into dashboards, and shared with teammates and vendors. So an A P I key, a password, or a token that lands in a log is effectively leaked. Redact or simply omit anything sensitive, including full user data. Keep your keys in environment variables, like ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY, and keep them out of every log line.

slides.title: Reach for tools
bullets: Good structured logs come first.
Sentry captures and groups exceptions.
A dashboard charts latency and error rate.
Layer tools on top, don't start with them.
slides.narration: Once your logs are structured, dedicated tools really earn their keep. Sentry captures exceptions with full stack traces and groups identical errors so you're not drowning in duplicates. A metrics dashboard charts latency and error rates over time, so you spot a slow creep before users complain. But the order matters: get good logs first, then layer tools on top. A tool can't surface signal you never emitted.
